passage:
"Jyoti, you're new to this newsroom, so let me tell you about my first editor," Naveen said, leaning back from his screen. "I was twenty-four. He shouted at juniors, took credit for our stories, and slept in the office like it was a medal. Half my batch burned out within two years.

"I learned a lot from him, mostly what not to do. When I got my first trainee, I promised myself three things. Check every fact twice, even at midnight. Put the trainee's name on the story they reported. Go home by nine unless the city is on fire.

"People laughed. They said I'd never get ahead. But my trainees stayed, and they're editors now. And I still enjoy this job, thirty years later.

"So when someone here tells you exhaustion is dedication, you tell them about me."

qa.q: What three promises did Naveen make when he got his first trainee?
qa.a: To check every fact twice even at midnight, to put the trainee's name on the story they reported, and to go home by nine unless the city was on fire.

qa.q: Why does Naveen want Jyoti to hear this story?
qa.a: He wants to protect her from believing that exhaustion and harshness equal dedication, because he saw his batch burn out under that belief.

qa.q: What could Jyoti do if a senior pressures her to work endless nights?
qa.a: She could keep high standards in her work while calmly holding reasonable hours, and look for mentors like Naveen who model that balance.

qa.q: How might Naveen's trainees have experienced working under him?
qa.a: They likely felt respected and safe to learn, since they got credit for their work and were not driven to burnout.

grounding: An elder recalls choosing high standards, fair credit and mentorship over a toxic, burnout-driven work culture in his twenties.

The wedding buffet was for eight hundred guests, and one of the hotel's cooks hadn't turned up. The head chef was yelling at everyone. Santosh, twenty-five and in charge of the fry station, had forty minutes.

Nilesh, the new trainee, held up a tray of old oil. "Chef says reuse this, it'll save time."

Santosh looked at the dark oil and shook his head. "It'll make the pakoras bitter and people's stomachs sick. Change it. I'll show you the fast way."

They worked side by side, Santosh talking him through each step without raising his voice. The pakoras went out on time.

At eleven, when the head chef told everyone to stay and deep-clean till two, Santosh finished his station properly, then said, "I'm on at six tomorrow, Chef. I'm going home." Nilesh watched him leave, surprised.

qa.q: What did Nilesh want to reuse to save time?
qa.a: He wanted to reuse a tray of old oil because the chef said it would save time.

qa.q: How can you tell Santosh felt steady under pressure?
qa.a: He explained the steps to Nilesh without raising his voice, even while the head chef was yelling and a cook was missing.

qa.q: What did Santosh model for Nilesh in this rush?
qa.a: He showed that you can keep quality and safety standards, teach patiently, and still protect your rest when the job is done.

qa.q: Why might Nilesh be surprised when Santosh leaves?
qa.a: In that kitchen, staying late whenever the head chef says seems normal, so seeing someone calmly hold a limit is new to him.

grounding: Shows a young cook keeping professional standards, mentoring a trainee and refusing burnout despite a toxic, rushed kitchen.

passage:
14 November

Long day but a good one. Our heritage walk group finally got permission to clean the old stepwell behind the tehsil office. Twenty of us turned up at seven with gloves and sacks. Vaibhav brought his students from the government school, and I spent an hour showing them the carvings: the elephants, the woman carrying water pots. One boy asked, "Didi, who made this?" I said, "People from this town, three hundred years ago. And now it's your job to look after it." He looked at the stone like it belonged to him. That was my favourite moment.

In the afternoon I helped at the voter registration camp near the market. Only eleven people came, which was disappointing.

I'm tired, but I feel like I spent today on something that will last. Next month: the kids make a guidebook.

— Gargi

qa.q: How many people came to the voter registration camp?
qa.a: Only eleven people came to the camp near the market.

qa.q: What does Gargi mean when she says she spent the day on something that will last?
qa.a: She feels her effort matters beyond today, because caring for the stepwell and teaching children passes the town's heritage and civic habits forward.

qa.q: How could Gargi get more people to the next registration camp?
qa.a: She could ask the students or local shopkeepers to spread the word, or hold it alongside a heritage event people already enjoy.

qa.q: How might the boy who asked who made the stepwell see the town now?
qa.a: He seems to feel the heritage belongs to him, which may make him more likely to protect it as he grows up.

grounding: A diary entry shows a young woman preserving local heritage, supporting civic processes and guiding the next generation.

passage:
Tushar's day in Jalna began before light. He helped his father, stiff from arthritis, to the bench outside and brought him tea and his pills in the order the doctor had written. Then he walked the field boundary where he had planted neem saplings last monsoon; six of the ten had survived.

At ten, three younger farmers from the next village came to see his drip lines. Pallavi, the youngest, had lost half her soybean crop last year to dry weeks. Tushar walked her through each pipe and valve, then said, "Don't copy me exactly. Your soil holds water better. Try two rows first."

That evening his father asked why he bothered with the neem trees. "They won't give shade for years."

Tushar poured his father more tea. "Not for me, Baba. For whoever farms here next."

qa.q: How many of the ten neem saplings had survived?
qa.a: Six of the ten had survived.

qa.q: Why does Tushar bother planting trees that won't give shade for years?
qa.a: He is thinking of the future and wants the land to be better for whoever farms it after him.

qa.q: What was good about the way Tushar mentored Pallavi?
qa.a: He explained the system clearly but told her to adapt it to her own soil and start small, which respects her situation instead of just making her copy him.

qa.q: How might Tushar's father feel about his son's daily care?
qa.a: He may feel grateful and cared for, and perhaps also a little puzzled by his son's long-term thinking.

grounding: Shows a young farmer caring for an ageing parent, mentoring peers and planting for future generations in a rural setting.

passage:
In the apartment block in Da Nang, everyone knew Tuan's schedule. Mornings, he cooked congee for his grandmother and checked she'd taken her blood pressure tablets. Then the motorbike ride to the engineering office, where he was training two new graduates. Tariq, the newer one, still froze in client meetings, so Tuan let him present one slide at a time.

On Saturdays Tuan ran the building's sorting corner: plastics, paper, food scraps for the rooftop garden the residents had started. Only half the families used it properly yet.

"Why do you do all this?" Tariq asked one evening, helping him carry compost upstairs.

Tuan wiped his hands. "My grandmother raised me. You'll lead a team one day. And this city will belong to your kids." He shrugged, smiling. "It's all the same job, really."

qa.q: What did Tuan cook for his grandmother in the mornings?
qa.a: He cooked congee for her.

qa.q: What does Tuan mean when he says it is "all the same job"?
qa.a: He sees caring for his grandmother, training young colleagues and looking after the environment as one responsibility to the people before and after him.

qa.q: How did Tuan support Tariq's confidence in meetings?
qa.a: He let Tariq present one slide at a time, giving him small, manageable chances to grow.

qa.q: How might Tuan's grandmother see her grandson's care?
qa.a: She would likely feel loved and secure, and proud that the boy she raised now looks after her and others.

grounding: Shows a young man abroad caring for an elder, mentoring a junior and leading environmental care in his building.

passage: I'm Jyoti from next door. Yesterday I watched Sangeeta, who is fourteen months old, on her mother's lap. Her mother pointed to the parrot on the wire and said, "Look, tota!" Sangeeta turned, followed the finger, and found the bird. Then she looked back at her mother's face and squealed, as if checking, "You see it too?" Her mother laughed and nodded. I can't know what Sangeeta was thinking, but they seemed to share that parrot.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta's mother point to?
qa.a: She pointed to the parrot on the wire and said, "Look, tota!"

qa.q: Why might Sangeeta have looked back at her mother's face?
qa.a: She seemed to want to share the moment and check that her mother was seeing the same bird, though Jyoti cannot be sure.

qa.q: How could a caregiver build on moments like this?
qa.a: Point to interesting things, name them, and wait for the child to look and look back, then respond warmly to what she noticed.

qa.q: What is it like for Sangeeta's mother when Sangeeta squeals and looks back?
qa.a: She seems delighted, laughing and nodding, enjoying the shared moment with her daughter.

grounding: A neighbour observes a toddler following her mother's point to a bird and looking back to share focus.

Monday: Rajni pointed at a crow on the balcony. Kalyani, one year old, stared at Rajni's finger, not the crow.

Thursday: Rajni pointed again and said, "Kalyani, crow!" This time Kalyani's eyes slid along the finger and landed on the bird. "Ah!"

Two weeks later: A plane roared overhead. Kalyani pointed up herself, then twisted round to see Rajni's face. Rajni looked up. "Yes, plane!" Kalyani bounced, clapping.

qa.q: What did Kalyani look at on Monday when Rajni pointed?
qa.a: She stared at Rajni's finger, not the crow.

qa.q: How can you tell Kalyani wanted to share the plane with Rajni?
qa.a: She pointed up and then twisted round to see Rajni's face, and bounced and clapped when Rajni looked too.

qa.q: What small habit of Rajni's helped Kalyani learn?
qa.a: She kept pointing at things, naming them and following Kalyani's own pointing, giving her many chances to practise shared looking.

qa.q: What would change if Rajni had not looked up when Kalyani pointed?
qa.a: Kalyani would miss the shared moment, and she might point less often if no one responded 😔

grounding: Shows a toddler progressing over weeks from looking at a pointing finger to following and then starting a point herself.

On Tuesday, Mohit, two, watched Dadi ring the little brass bell during evening prayers in their Kolkata flat. Nobody thought he was paying attention.

On Thursday afternoon, Kiran found him in the corner by the prayer shelf. He had a steel spoon in one hand and was shaking it slowly, humming, eyes half closed, just like Dadi. Then he bowed his head so low he nearly toppled over.

Kiran covered her mouth to hide her laugh and called Dadi to come and see.

qa.q: What did Mohit use as a bell?
qa.a: He used a steel spoon, shaking it slowly and humming.

qa.q: Why did Kiran cover her mouth?
qa.a: She was trying to hide her laugh because Mohit's copy of Dadi was so sweet and funny.

qa.q: How could the family support Mohit's copying?
qa.a: They could invite him to join the prayers, give him a small safe role, and name what he is doing, so his imitation becomes shared learning.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel seeing Mohit copy her?
qa.a: She would probably feel touched and delighted that he noticed and wanted to be like her.

grounding: Shows a toddler copying a household ritual days after watching a grandparent.

The winter dark came early in Malmö, and Xin, eighteen months old, woke from her nap screaming. Her face was red and her fists were tight.

Lars picked her up and held her against his chest. He walked slowly around the kitchen, patting her back in a steady rhythm and humming the same low tune. "Shh, I've got you."

Her cries turned to hiccups. Her fingers uncurled on his sweater. After a few minutes she was quiet, one cheek on his shoulder, watching the window.

qa.q: What was Lars doing as he walked around the kitchen?
qa.a: He patted Xin's back in a steady rhythm and hummed the same low tune.

qa.q: What do Xin's uncurling fingers suggest about how she was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest her body was relaxing and she was beginning to feel safe and calm in Lars's arms.

qa.q: What worked well in how Lars soothed Xin?
qa.a: He used close holding, a slow steady walk, patting and a familiar tune, which a young child can lean on before she can calm herself.

qa.q: How might Lars feel as Xin quietens down?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and close to her once the crying turns to calm.

grounding: Shows a toddler abroad being calmed by a parent's touch, voice and rhythm.

passage: I'm Tarun, Vinita's uncle. Last Sunday she fell off the sofa at our house and howled. I tried talking fast and waving toys; it made things worse. Then her mother lifted her, rocked side to side, and sang the same short lullaby slowly, again and again. Her mother's hand made small circles on Vinita's back. Within a minute Vinita's crying slowed. She tucked her head under her mother's chin. I don't know exactly what changed inside her, but I noticed the slow rhythm did what my toys couldn't.

qa.q: What did Tarun try first when Vinita cried?
qa.a: He tried talking fast and waving toys, which made things worse.

qa.q: Why might Vinita have tucked her head under her mother's chin?
qa.a: She seemed to feel safe and comforted, looking for closeness as her body calmed, though Tarun cannot be sure what she felt.

qa.q: What could Tarun try next time Vinita is upset?
qa.a: He could hold her close, slow down, and use a calm voice and steady rocking instead of fast talk and toys.

qa.q: How might Vinita's mother feel when she calms her daughter?
qa.a: She would likely feel steady and connected, glad that her touch and song can settle Vinita.

grounding: An uncle observes a toddler being calmed by her mother's rocking, song and touch.

"Press, beta," he said. She pressed it. The button glowed and the doors slid shut. Hansa gasped.

On the path to the well in their village near Nashik, Mahima, two, would not stop asking. "What that?" She pointed at a goat.

"Bakri," said Jyoti Mausi.

"Bakri!" Then she pointed at a cart, a bucket, a red flower. "What that? What that?" Each new word she repeated loudly.

At the well a dog barked and she hid behind Jyoti's legs. "Scared," she whispered, a new word. Jyoti crouched. "Yes, you felt scared. He's just saying hello."

qa.q: What was the first thing Mahima pointed at on the path?
qa.a: She pointed at a goat, and Jyoti Mausi named it bakri.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when the dog barked, and how did she show it?
qa.a: She felt scared, hiding behind Jyoti's legs and whispering the new word "scared."

qa.q: What did Jyoti do well when Mahima named her fear?
qa.a: She crouched down, repeated the feeling word back and gently explained the dog, helping Mahima connect words to both things and feelings.

qa.q: What is it like for Jyoti Mausi to answer "What that?" again and again?
qa.a: It might be a little tiring, but she seems patient and pleased by how quickly Mahima is learning words.

grounding: Shows a toddler's burst of new words, repeated 'what's that?' questions and naming a feeling, in a village setting.

At the Saturday market in Kraków, two-year-old Olga rode on Clara's hip and pointed at everything. "What's dat?"

"Plums," said Clara.

"Plums!" Olga reached for one. Then the cheese man, the balloons, a dog in a scarf. "What's dat? What's dat?" Clara named them all, laughing.

Near the bread stall Olga suddenly frowned at a crying baby. "Baby sad," she said. Clara nodded. "Yes, the baby is sad. Maybe hungry." Olga nodded seriously.

qa.q: What was the first thing Clara named for Olga?

qa.q: What does Olga saying "Baby sad" show about her?
qa.a: It shows she is noticing other people's feelings and beginning to find words for them, not just for objects.

qa.q: How could Clara keep supporting Olga's language?
qa.a: She can keep naming things and feelings, add a little more, as she did with "maybe hungry," and answer the questions patiently.

qa.q: Why might Clara enjoy the market trip despite all the questions?
qa.a: Hearing Olga learn new words so fast and seeing her notice feelings is delightful, which is why Clara keeps laughing.

grounding: Shows a toddler abroad rapidly naming objects and a feeling while asking what things are.
